description.narrative: GLTN partners jointly developed a GLTN Phase Strategy (2018-2030) through an intensive strategic review that involved a wide range of partners and role players in the land sector, including the GLTN Steering Committee and the International Advisory Board. The GLTN Phase Strategy was endorsed during the GLTN partners’ meeting in April 2018 in Nairobi, setting a shared vision and direction for the Network - a world in which everyone enjoys secure land rights. The partners agreed that the spirit of the GLTN Phase Strategy would be translated into action through a joint programme and that there would be two programme cycles. This document presents the GLTN Phase 3 programme that covers the period 2019-2023. The five-year programme budget is 45 million USD. It will be jointly implemented by GLTN partners and the Secretariat. The Secretariat, hosted by UN- Habitat within the Land, Housing and Shelter Section in the Urban Practices Branch, will also facilitate the administrative and financial aspects of the programme. The GLTN Phase 3 2019 - 2023 programme aims at realizing the 2030 goal of improving tenure security for all. This will be achieved through a) accelerating reforms of the land sector by fostering global, regional and national discourse on responsible land governance and transformative land policies; b) institutionalizing inclusive, gender-responsive and fit-for-purpose land tools to scale up tenure security interventions; c) monitoring land-related commitments and obligations by mobilizing international, regional and national partners to track progress and build evidence; and d) sharing and developing capacities, knowledge, research and resources on land tenure security among the Network partners. The programme will focus on five priority contexts of intervention, these are: 1) Recognizing customary and indigenous land rights and the potential of communal and group tenure systems to increase land-based investment and improve livelihoods 2)Improving tenure security in informal settlement and slum contexts 3) Addressing land-tenure security within the urban-rural nexus 4) Reducing land rights’ vulnerabilities to climate-change impacts 5) Securing the land rights of affected communities in conflict-affected contexts. The programme contributes to the achievements of several global development commitments. Five of the 17 SDGs (1, 2, 5, 11 and 15) make specific reference to and advance the role of land in sustainable development, with SDG Indicator 1.4.2 directly tracking progress in strengthening tenure security. The New Urban Agenda focuses squarely on tenure security, housing and community development as key requirements for sustainable, inclusive and efficient cities; envisages cities and human settlements that fulfil their social function, including the social and ecological function of land; and confirms the importance of the continuum of land rights approach and the role of GLTN. More specifically, the programme directly contributes to the NUA commitments specified in paragraphs 13 and 35. The Voluntary Guidelines on the Responsible Governance of Tenure have put land tenure at the centre of the global efforts to secure tenure rights for food security and protect natural resources. In the African Union Declaration on land issues and challenges, states parties resolve to: i) ensure that land laws provide for equitable access to land and related resources among all land users, including the youth and other landless and vulnerable groups such as displaced persons; ii) strengthen security of land tenure for women who require special attention. The programme also contributes to the implementation of the following UN-Habitat Governing Council Resolutions: i) resolution on sustainable urban development through expanding equitable access to land, housing, basic services and infrastructure (GC.23-17); ii) resolution on implementation of the Strategic Plan for 2014-2019 (HSP/GC/25/L.6), which “requests the Executive Director to continue to support and reinforce the coordination of the efforts of the United Nations system, through the Global Land Tool Network, to bring coherence and conflict-sensitive approaches to land issues, including through a plurality of land tenure systems for all segments of society and alternative forms of land administration”. Lastly, the programme contributes to the four sub-programmes and UN-Habitat Strategic Plan Domains of Change, with more substantive contributions on ‘reduced spatial inequality and poverty in communities across the urban-rural continuum’, particularly under Outcome 2 – Increased and secure access to land, and adequate and affordable housing.
